extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors of algebraic geometry (Math 216 / first serious-year level); self-learners
extracted.subtask_description: A one-year, first-serious-course textbook/course for students to learn foundational algebraic geometry (commutative algebra, category theory, schemes), usable both in a course and for guided self-study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite mathematical background
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers should have basic notions in commutative ring theory (ideals, prime and maximal ideals, localization), familiarity with tensor products and exact sequences of A-modules, experience with the structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a PID, and some field theory; some previous exposure to topology is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some experience in related areas (topology, geometry, complex analysis, number theory, ...) will help intuition. The text uses notation (A, m) or (A, m, k) for local rings (m maximal ideal, k = A/m residue field). Suggested references for background: [E], [AtM], [Mat2], [Al] for commutative algebra; [Wei] for homological algebra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about foundational (set-theoretic) issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The book will not concern itself with subtle foundational/set-theoretic issues (universes, size issues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reader genuinely needs those subtleties addressed, they should consult other sources (e.g., KS2, §1.1). The text adopts the pragmatic stance of omitting these set-theoretic digressions to focus on core material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Starred-section reading priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections are marked with stars to indicate optionality: ⋆ sections are optional and worth knowing on a second or third reading; ⋆⋆ sections should not be read on a first pass (they are supplementary or not essential).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starred sections are not necessarily harder, merely less central. Be aware of double-starred sections' existence but skip them on first reading unless you really want to dig deeper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core goals: scope and depth
rubrics_metrics.description: The intent is to cover a canon completely and rigorously with enough examples and calculations to develop intuition — essentially the content of a second course, but presented as a first (challenging) introduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material is chosen so that the core should be digestible over a single year; after a year, readers should have broad familiarity with foundations, know interesting examples and their details, and be ready to attend seminars. The book is not encyclopedic and makes hard choices about included topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-containedness and explicit proofs ('if you use it, you must prove it')
rubrics_metrics.description: The book aims to be as self-contained as possible: if a fact is used, it should be proved or developed in the text rather than deferred to distant references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This increases the density and sophistication of the text (making it harder), but reduces prerequisites and prevents students from being thrown by missing background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intended balance: prioritize core foundations and intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: The book seeks to build intuition for the machinery (categorical thinking, universal properties) and emphasize what is essential rather than exhaustive coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation is local rather than global (e.g., explains why to think categorically and how to do it). Examples and exercises are used to demonstrate advantages of appropriate generality rather than intimidate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use in courses and instructor discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: The book is usable for a course but the instructor should shape the course's personality and select which inessential topics to include.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With a good course, some students may leave early and still get useful material; instructors choose which 'inessential' topics are important for their point of view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice for self-learners
rubrics_metrics.description: The book can be used for independent study, but most learners will benefit from reading in a group or having someone to ask questions to (both 'stupid' and smart questions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most mortals cannot learn algebraic geometry fully on their own; exercises are central to building understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercises and examples are central
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises are central to building intuition and mastering the material; many examples are given to develop familiarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal language may be used when helpful. See section 0.0.1 for comments about exercises. The pedagogy emphasizes working through details of examples, not just vague intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limitation: analytic aspects omitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytic aspects of algebraic geometry are essentially ignored or only treated in passing without proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an 'algebraic algebraic geometry' book — analytic/complex-analytic viewpoints are not the focus and are not developed here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation and nonmathematical conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain words and notations are used idiosyncratically: e.g., 'Unimportant' means 'unimportant for the current exposition'; local ring notation (A, m) or (A, m, k); star markings indicate reading priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should note these conventions; other words may be used idiosyncratically as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation style: begin with familiar examples, then abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: The author will begin by telling things the reader already knows and describing essential features of examples, then abstract those features into definitions (e.g., define product via universal property after revisiting product of sets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach encourages seeing why precise definitions deserve their names and using universal properties to show uniqueness up to unique isomorphism; it favors motivation-by-example and abstraction only as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of substantial proofs with reading guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Important theorems may be given full proofs (e.g., Krull's Principal Ideal Theorem) but marked to indicate whether they are appropriate for first reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A double-star indicates a proof or section that the author does not expect readers to read unless they really want to; such sections might be skimmed to see they are accessible without detailed reading on first pass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoffs and explicit acceptance of limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The book explicitly accepts that balancing its goals is impossible and that it must give up other desiderata in order to focus on its stated aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are no other goals beyond the stated core aims; readers and instructors should not expect coverage beyond the chosen scope.
